newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan export ban on pork seen hiking jobless rate.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan export ban on pork seen hiking jobless rate.

text.p: Economists on Monday predicted Taiwan's pork export crisis would dent recent employment gains, likely causing up to 100,000 layoffs and pushing the 1997 jobless rate up to 3.0 percent -- above the government's target.
The cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development has set a 1997 unemployment target of 2.6 percent.

The cabinet-level Council of Agriculture on March 20 slapped a temporary ban on all exports of fresh and frozen pork due to an outbreak of the deadly contagious foot-and-mouth disease, a hard blow to a multibillion-dollar export sector.
Japan and South Korea -- the main importers of Taiwan pork -- responded by banning pork imports from Taiwan indefinitely to protect their herds.
Officials said the crisis would fuel unemployment.
"The ban on pork exports will worsen the jobless situation," Cheng Shuo-liang, a section-chief at the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, told Reuters.
"This will reverse what had been an improving trend and push the jobless rate up to around three percent for 1997," he said.
In February, Cheng and several private economists had forecast unemployment would fall in 1997 to around 2.5 percent as a gathering economic recovery created more jobs.
Cheng said the pork crisis impact would first be seen in April's jobless rate, to be announced in late May.
"April joblessness likely will rise to above 3.0 percent," Cheng said. "And since the pork export ban will also hit related industries, its impact will be quite long-term."

Cheng's agency said on Monday that Taiwan's unemployment rate was 2.97 percent in February, up from 2.68 percent in January and slightly above an average forecast of 2.81 percent from a March 21 Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists.
Economists said the pork crisis could throw 50,000-100,000 workers out of jobs, boosting the jobless rate by 0.5-0.6 percentage points.

Joblessness held close to 1.5 percent in 1991-1994 but rose to 1.79 percent in 1995 and pushed above 3.0 percent in August, September and October of 1996. The rate fell back below 3.0 percent in November and December.
It was 2.60 percent for all of 1996, a 10-year high.
"The jobless rate may rise as much as to 3.2 percent if we estimate half of the direct work force affected by the pork export ban," said Deniel Chen, chief economist at Chinatrust Commercial Bank.
But in fact, he said, many of the workers in the hog industry see their hog business as a part-time job and they could turn to other businesses.
"So the real impact will not be so big as we have anticipated," Chen said.
The agriculture council said those directly employed in the hog industry was about 100,000, and that for the related industries the total was some 700,000.
But while the ban on pork exports would hurt Taiwan's exports and increase the jobless rate, it should have little impact on the island's overall economy, economists said.

"The impact on the overall economy will be limited because we can use the original work force (in the hog industry) to generate other output, and we still have certain domestic demand for pork," Chen said.
"The trend of our slowly recovering economy should continue," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
